claims.claim: The progressive-sync failure in T-27949 is unobservable in production today: the rollout reports complete because status.applicationStatus stays Healthy and syncDesiredApplications never creates a sync operation, so no operation failure, no error, and no transition log is emitted (the report notes controller logs were at warn level and emitted nothing). The only measurement that would surface it — 'how much time did it take to complete step X' and 'which Applications is it waiting for' — is still an open request in T-27846, unimplemented. Until those metrics exist, a silently incomplete RollingSync is detectable only by manually diffing each child Application's status.sync.status against the ApplicationSet's applicationStatus.

T-28927 defines the remaining scope for promoting Progressive Sync from beta to Stable as two GitHub label queries (open enhancement and bug issues), which is a count of unclosed tickets, not evidence that the feature is 'tested and validated with various use cases' as the argoproj feature-status definition it quotes requires. No progressive-sync telemetry exists to supply that evidence: the metrics that would show trigger latency, per-step duration, and refresh volume are exactly what T-27846 is still requesting. The stability promotion therefore depends on T-27846 landing first without saying so, and as written can be declared satisfied by closing tickets rather than by any recorded number.

The PRD's Reverse deletionOrder is specified as 'waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next', but nothing in the corpus records the duration or completion of that wait. T-28511 shows the failure mode this hides: a child stuck in Progressing means the wait never completes and the controller restarts the wave, which surfaces only as an Application visibly flipping between Deleting and Syncing in the UI. The metrics requested in T-27846 cover RollingSync step timing, not deletion steps, so shipping deletionOrder adds a new blocking wait with no per-step duration metric and no stuck-deletion counter behind it.

note-2's standing mitigation — switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce before deleting any child by hand — is enforced only by the incident runbook. The PRD places deletionOrder in ApplicationSetStrategy with no validation beyond correlating Reverse to a rollingSync order, so there is no controller-level check or alert that fires when an operator hand-deletes a child while deletionOrder is Reverse. Compliance with the operational rule is therefore unmeasurable: no signal distinguishes a correctly-mitigated manual teardown from one that will trigger the wave-restart loop, and the first evidence is the loop itself.

T-26443's proposed freshness gate — block sync when the hydrated files' hydrator.metadata is older than a timestamp annotation on the app — has no field to compare against. RFC-002's hydrator.metadata JSON contains commands, drySHA, commitAuthor, commitMessage, and repoURL, but no hydration or commit timestamp, even though commitTime exists in the CommitManifests message and the README template. The staleness this guards against is unobservable for the same reason: a push-to-stage app that auto-syncs an old manifest reports Synced and Healthy, so nothing records how stale the applied revision was.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode explicitly relies on 'some external system' to move changes to the deployment branch, and note-1 records that this system is still a shell script that nobody owns. T-26443 is the measured consequence: auto-sync applies whatever the stage branch last held because the promoter has not moved the fresh manifests yet. Promotion lag — the interval between a hydrated commit landing on the stage branch and its arrival on the deployment branch — is the number that would size this exposure, and no component in the corpus records it, because the promoter sits outside Argo CD entirely.

note-1 records as a firm decision that impersonation rolls out behind a per-project flag rather than fleet-wide, but RFC-001 states as a goal that the feature can be enabled or disabled only at the system level, applicable to all Argo CD Applications, and every enablement example in the RFC patches the single argocd-cm key application.sync.impersonation.enabled. The decided rollout unit does not exist as a setting, which also means per-project rollout state is unrecordable: there is no field to read to answer which projects have impersonation on.

The gate note-1 puts on impersonation rollout — nobody flips a project until the diff story is fixed — has no exit measurement. RFC-001's only observability claim is that Kubernetes audit trail events capture both the actual and impersonating user, which records the identity used for the sync operation; the diff path is not part of the sync operation and, per T-28695, runs as the cluster Secret credential instead of the mapped destinationServiceAccounts identity. Audit trails therefore cannot show whether a project's diffs run under the narrow identity, so 'the diff story is fixed' is unfalsifiable from the signals the design provides.

T-28695 carries a measured result for its workaround — ServerSideDiff=false across roughly 20 monitoring charts, including StatefulSets with volumeClaimTemplates, produced no cosmetic OutOfSync and required no ignoreDifferences — while T-26271, which the ticket identifies as the same forbidden-dry-run error string in the argocd-server in-cluster path, carries no measurement at all and its reporter is still chasing the broad cluster Secret credential. note-1 holds the root cause (with impersonation on, diff runs as the destination service account, which lacks patch on cluster-scoped resources) but records that nobody has written it onto the ticket. The diagnosis exists only in call notes, so the rate of impersonation-caused CI diff failures is knowledge nobody can query.

T-28695 warns that making Server-Side Diff the default would put every external-cluster user into a ComparisonError with no obvious cause, but sizing that blast radius before the change ships requires a baseline that does not exist anywhere in the corpus: a count of Applications whose destination is an external cluster, cross-referenced with impersonation enablement and per-App ServerSideDiff annotations. RFC-001 offers no such inventory — destinationServiceAccounts is matched at reconcile time by first-valid-glob against server and namespace, and nothing aggregates which destinations resolve to a narrow standing credential. The before/after comparison for the default flip has no before.

T-27875 and T-27949 are the same class of unobservable defect in two controllers: in both, the bug's outcome is that no sync operation is ever created, so no operation fails, no retry counter increments, and the app simply remains OutOfSync while the reporting layer says otherwise (T-27875's app stays OutOfSync indefinitely with only a debug-grade 'Already attempted sync' log line; T-27949's ApplicationSet stays Healthy). Any monitoring built on sync success and failure counts is blind to both, because the missing event is the symptom. The metric that would catch this class is a per-Application OutOfSync-duration measure, which nothing in the corpus proposes — T-27846's requested metrics stop at progressive-sync step timing.

note-2 records that each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave on hydrated repos, and T-27949 confirms the mechanism from the pilot side: every hydration cycle lands a fresh commit on the hydrated branch and each is picked up as a source change. RFC-002 makes this rate structural, since a single dry commit fans out to a commit on up to three environment branches. The size of the effect is precisely T-27846's third requested metric, 'how much Application refresh were caused by the ApplicationSet', which is still unimplemented — so the debounce that note-2 makes a precondition for lifting the pilot restriction would ship with no measurement of how many restarts it removed.

note-1 deprioritizes the hydrator History and Rollback work to next quarter while moving the dev pair onto the progressive sync deletion loop, which means the recovery path for a mid-deletion failure is manual. T-27327 shows what is being deferred: rollback under the source hydrator would be a checkout of old rendered manifests pushed forward onto the sync branch, and its stated goal was to add enough commit metadata for a promotion system to judge whether later promotion is safe. Without it, no time-to-recover baseline is captured before the deletion feature ships, so the PRD's claim of 'No immediate Risks to consider' rests on an unmeasured recovery path rather than a recorded one.

The strategy document states twice that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented and that teardown remains a manual operator action performed one Application at a time, yet T-28511 reproduces a bug on v3.3.9 against an ApplicationSet that already sets strategy.deletionOrder, and the PRD specifies that field as new work. The roadmap's out-of-scope statement is therefore already contradicted by shipped behavior in a user's report, and nothing ties the roadmap text to a release-state signal that would have flagged the divergence; note-2 records the disagreement being raised and left without an owner.

T-29001 argues that the global ARGOCD_K8S_CLIENT_QPS of 50 and burst of 100 overwhelm edge clusters and starve large ones, but the proposal specifies only the configuration surface (Cluster Secret annotations or a typed config field with fallback to argocd-cmd-params-cm) and no per-cluster observation of API throttling or reconcile latency. Operators would be asked to choose a per-cluster number with no recorded before-value, and no after-value to show the tuning helped: the only telemetry requested anywhere in the corpus, T-27846's progressive-sync metrics, is scoped to ApplicationSet step timing and is itself still open.

RFC-002 makes the hydrator.metadata file the provenance record that external systems, such as a PR-based promoter, are meant to read when deciding what to promote, and its Security Considerations section defers the question of git permissions and branch protection entirely. T-28239 names the gap that leaves: the commit server pushes unsigned commits, so if signature verification is enabled on the hydrated branch, Argo CD rejects its own output. The ticket's fail-fast rule — the commit server refuses to start if the configured key is missing or invalid, rather than falling back silently — is the only observable in this area, and it makes misconfiguration detectable at startup instead of as an unexplained rejected push.

The PRD's Non-Goals section states that the custom deletion strategy will be unsupported while the UI will not say so, leaving a configuration field that accepts input and ignores it silently. Nothing records how often that happens: the strategy document already notes that first-class ApplicationSet UI/CLI/API support does not cover managing deletion order of child applications, so the silently-ignored value has no validation error, no warning, and no counter behind it. An operator who sets deletionOrder: Custom on a teardown discovers the setting was inert only when the applications delete in the AllAtOnce pattern instead.

T-27833 and T-24578 both ask for capability that the impersonation and hydrator designs place out of reach at different granularities, and neither can be checked against a recorded signal. T-27833 needs the control plane to apply namespace resources while the impersonated service account does not, but RFC-001 fixes the impersonation identity at the Application level rather than per resource, using Application.spec.destination.namespace for every resource in the Application, so no per-resource identity is recorded to audit against. T-24578 needs deletion ordering across multiple ApplicationSets, which the PRD's deletionOrder cannot express because it derives its order from a single ApplicationSet's rollingSync steps.
